title: Real beauty
hook: to a young man with elaborate hair: beauty is in excellence, not in grooming (Discourses 3.1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: no scorekeeping, the puppies and the piece of meat. Did you do something for a friend without counting it? Day four hundred sixteen.

One morning a young student of public speaking walked into Epictetus' classroom with his hair arranged in elaborate curls, his whole appearance polished to a shine. You can picture the other students glancing at each other. Epictetus hesitated. Should he say something? If I keep quiet, he thought, this young man may someday say: Epictetus saw me walk in like that, and never said a word. So he spoke. But he didn't mock. He asked a question about dogs. Today: real beauty.
screen: `HAIR IN ELABORATE CURLS.` → `SHOULD HE SAY SOMETHING?` → `A QUESTION ABOUT DOGS.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book three, chapter one. Tell me, Epictetus says to the young man, don't you think some dogs are beautiful? Some horses? Yes. Is it the same thing that makes each of them beautiful, or something different? Think about it. A dog is beautiful when it's excellent as a dog. A horse when it's excellent as a horse. A beautiful racehorse and a beautiful sheepdog aren't beautiful in the same way; each is beautiful by being very good at being what it is. So what makes a human being beautiful? Excellence as a human. And what is that? Justice. Self-control. Self-mastery. Being faithful and fair. If you want to be beautiful, Epictetus tells him, work on those. Then comes the line that turns it from a lecture into a kindness. You aren't your hair, he says, or your skin. You're your will, your choosing self. Make that beautiful, and you will be beautiful. Notice he's not against looking after yourself. Elsewhere in the Discourses he's quite firm that students should keep clean and not put people off. His point is about where the real work goes. A morning in front of the mirror shapes the hair. A morning of being honest, patient and fair shapes the person. Only one of those, he says, is the beauty that belongs to a human being.
screen: `WHAT MAKES A DOG BEAUTIFUL?` · `EXCELLENT AT BEING WHAT IT IS.` · `JUSTICE, SELF-CONTROL, FAITHFULNESS.` · `YOU AREN'T YOUR HAIR.` · then, large: `REAL BEAUTY.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Think of someone you know who is beautiful in Epictetus' sense: honest, kind, steady, fair. Picture their face, and notice that what makes it beautiful to you isn't really the features. Let yourself feel grateful for them. Then choose one quality of theirs you could name to them today. Not their outfit or their haircut. Their character. Then ask, quietly, which of those qualities you'd like someone to see in you. The bell holds the time.
Real beauty. Epictetus to a carefully groomed young man: each creature is beautiful by excelling at what it is, and a human's excellence is justice and self-control.
Your line: real beauty. Today, compliment someone's character, not their looks: their honesty, their patience, their kindness. Day four hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: People who take this chapter to heart often make a point of praising others for their character rather than their appearance, and give their own mornings to character as well as grooming.

myth: Epictetus mocks the young man's hair in front of the class
he asks him a gentle question about dogs and horses.
he says each creature is beautiful by being excellent at what it is
a dog as a dog, a horse as a horse, a human as a human.
Epictetus tells his students not to bother keeping clean
elsewhere he insists they keep clean; his point is where the real work goes.

fork.setup: you're Epictetus. a student walks in with elaborately styled hair. what do you do?
options: ask him what makes a dog or a horse beautiful.
fork.reveal: he worried the young man would one day say Epictetus never told him, so he asked about dogs and horses, and led him to human excellence.

original.note: Greek kallos: beauty (as in calligraphy, beautiful writing); 3.1 asks what makes each creature beautiful.

trapdoor: what you thought: beauty is only skin deep.
what it means: each thing is beautiful by excelling at what it is, and a human's excellence is character.
what a scholar hears: the Greek word for excellence, aretē, applied to horses and knives as well as people, so 'beautiful as a human' means 'excellent as a human' for Epictetus.

notes: Discourses 3.1 paraphrased: young rhetoric student with elaborately dressed hair; dogs, horses and their beauty as excellence; human excellence as justice, temperance, self-control; 'you are not flesh or hair, but will'; Epictetus' worry that the young man would later say he was never told. Confirm.
Discourses 4.11 cited for the point that Epictetus wants students clean and not offensive to others. Confirm.
